paras: The attempted lynching of Isaiah Fountain took place at Easton, Talbot County, Maryland, in April 1919, when crowds of white farmers tried to seize a Black farmer from Trappe who was on trial for an alleged criminal assault on a white girl. Fountain escaped during a rush on his police escort, was recaptured in Delaware, and was convicted and sentenced to death; his lawyer appealed on the ground that the mob had made a fair trial impossible. The Baltimore Afro-American, which sent its own correspondents, covered the case for three months and treated the trial as nearly a lynching.

Fountain, reported as 27 and the owner of a 110-acre farm, was charged with assaulting Bertha Simpson, a white girl the Afro-American gave as 14, on April 1, and was arrested nine days later. When word reached Easton that he had been caught, crowds gathered at the jail and the railroad station "intent upon taking him to the prison and stringing him to the first tree." The judge, state's attorney and sheriff vowed to die before letting him be lynched, and he was held in Baltimore until the trial.

His return to Easton drew thousands of farmers, and before dawn on the trial's Monday some four hundred filled the courtyard, one carrying a new rope. When Judge Adkins closed the night session to spectators, the crowd grew, and as court adjourned at about ten o'clock a rush was made on the police amid cries of "get the Nigger" and "lynch the brute."

In the confusion Fountain fled up a side street, while a crowd that took the escape for a ruse held the sheriff at the jail for three hours. After a hunt through two states he was recaptured on April 23 at Hartley, Delaware, by deputy sheriffs. After an Afro-American telegram to Governor Emerson C. Harrington, troops reached Easton, and the paper reported that some mob leaders had been sworn in as deputies to hunt the prisoner.

Fountain was convicted of criminal assault, sentenced to death and lodged in the Baltimore City Jail; according to his lawyer's brief, the jury deliberated less than five minutes. The Afro-American's correspondent reported that no arrests of mob members were made. His counsel, Eugene O'Dunne, a white Baltimore lawyer, appealed, arguing before the Court of Appeals on June 24 that mob violence had been done to Fountain in custody; no decision is reported in the coverage.
White residents of Easton, without disputing the Afro-American's account, asked for its correspondent's name, and a rumor that a Trappe teacher, William H. Potts, had written it put him in danger.

Nearly all the coverage came from the Afro-American, whose staff correspondence ran under headlines such as "Few Officers Try to Hold Mob of Thousands." Its correspondent, kept out of the press box by Judge Adkins, wrote that Fountain was "lynched in spirit, if he is not actually," and the paper asked whether Easton was "Better Than the South." Editorials blamed Easton's whites and Governor Harrington, contrasting his "weak proclamation" with the troops he had sent to Annapolis for the John Snowden case.

After the conviction the paper turned on the defense, asking why O'Dunne had not sought a change of venue and why he had offered $250 of Fountain's fee for his recapture, and it called the case "the mob trial at Easton." O'Dunne replied that the only other venue was Chestertown, and the paper allowed that a quick conviction may have saved Fountain's life.

Elsewhere the Black press ran brief items; the Ohio State Monitor reported the recapture of a "colored" prisoner charged with attacking a 13-year-old white girl. A May item on Judge Adkins's $5,000 reward ran in the St. Louis Argus, the Omaha Monitor, the Wisconsin Weekly Blade and the Colorado Statesman, the last headed "Reward of $5,000 to Prevent a Lynching."

Simpson's age was given as 13 or 14, while people the Afro-American said had known her put her at 17 or 18. The Afro-American described the $5,000 reward as one for Fountain's recapture after his escape, while the wire item, datelined in May after his conviction, described it as a reward for bringing him into court uninjured.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Isaiah Fountain
bases: White crowds gathered at Easton to seize a Black prisoner on trial for an alleged assault, rushed his police escort with cries of 'lynch the brute', and he escaped; no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching (A6, A10, A34).

A crowd reported in the thousands tried to take Fountain under the pretext of punishing an alleged assault on a white girl (A6, A10, A34), but he escaped, was recaptured and was tried, convicted and appealed; no killing is reported (A13, A32), so it is an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The mob scenes and attempt come only from the Baltimore Afro-American's own correspondents (A6, A8, A10, A34); the Ohio State Monitor wire item confirms only the escape and recapture (A12), and the ANP reward item implies a threat to the prisoner (A21).

accounts.label: Afro-American staff correspondent
accounts.gist: Thousands of armed and threatening farmers besieged the courthouse; when the night session was closed they rushed the police with cries of 'lynch the brute' and Fountain escaped in the confusion.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Fountain, 'colored', escaped after the first day of his trial on the charge of attacking a 13-year-old white girl and was recaptured at Hartley, Del., by deputy sheriffs.

accounts.label: Defense appeal (O'Dunne)
accounts.gist: Mob violence was done to Fountain in custody during his trial, he fled for want of protection, the identification was weak, and the jury's under-five-minute verdict followed 'the will of the mob'.

accounts.label: ANP item on the judge's reward
accounts.gist: Judge Adkins offered $5,000 for bringing Fountain into court uninjured and told the sheriff to deputize every man in the county to protect him.

framing.detail: The Afro-American headlined 'Fountain Has Small Chance for Justice' and 'Few Officers Try to Hold Mob of Thousands', said Fountain was 'lynched in spirit', and blamed Easton's whites and Governor Harrington.
Its editorials then questioned defense counsel O'Dunne over the change of venue and his fee, calling the case 'the mob trial at Easton'.
Papers outside Maryland ran only brief wire items: the recapture, and Judge Adkins's reward, headed 'Must Bring Negro to Court Uninjured' or 'Judge Offers $5,000 Reward for Prisoner'.
